section_summary: The section closes an English discussion of Japanese municipal government and contains a Japanese text on citizenship and local self-government. It then turns to reports on local autonomy conferences, the sixth special Diet session, and a survey of political opinion. The final documents concern Philippine foreign policy toward Japan and an enclosed radio address, which continues beyond page 396.

subfiles.title: Discussion of municipal committees, boards, and local government
subfiles.about: The concluding pages explain Japanese municipal police, education, inspection, and other agencies.
subfiles.summary: The text describes the powers and public responsibilities of police commissions, local boards of education, and optional inspection committees. It urges sound municipal finance, restraint in creating agencies, scrutiny of their performance, and serious consideration of their recommendations.

subfiles.title: Japanese text on the city and the citizen
subfiles.about: The text discusses local self-government and citizens’ duties in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Beginning with the development of representative city government, the text explains citizenship under Japan’s constitution and Local Autonomy Law. It urges informed voting, payment and oversight of taxes, petitions, direct contact with officials, and participation in civic associations. The concluding pages call for active citizens and responsive municipal government.

subfiles.title: Discussion of a local autonomy conference at Uji-Yamada
subfiles.about: A surviving concluding page reports Vice Consul Magistretti’s observations from a conference in Mie Prefecture.
subfiles.summary: Attendees criticized local taxation; Magistretti expected a Japanese form of democracy to develop.

subfiles.title: Opening of Sixth Special Diet Session
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch assesses the government’s legislative agenda and opposition at the sixth special Diet session.
subfiles.summary: Sebald outlines budget and tax proposals, party strengths in both Diet houses, and likely disputes over wages, exchange rates, deflation, and a peace conference. He expects Yoshida’s majority to carry its program while noting growing cooperation among center parties and a more aggressive Social Democratic opposition.

subfiles.title: Civil Affairs Conference at Ogaki
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sebald forwards Finn’s report on an Ogaki conference promoting participation in local government.
subfiles.summary: Sebald forwards Finn’s report and highlights its favorable assessment of local autonomy despite financial difficulties.

subfiles.title: Civil Affairs Conference at Ogaki
subfiles.about: Finn reports on the October 21–22 local autonomy conference in Ogaki.
subfiles.summary: Finn describes lectures and group discussions attended by local officials and citizens. Participants showed interest in American practice and generally understood reforms, but identified finance as the chief obstacle and raised concerns about Communist use of recall petitions. Finn found the conference uneven and argued that reducing occupation civil affairs teams could strengthen Japanese responsibility for local decisions.

subfiles.title: Transmitting Copy of Survey of Political Trends
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The office transmits data from an Asahi survey of Japanese political attitudes.
subfiles.summary: Transmits a copy of survey data prepared for SCAP’s public opinion research division.

subfiles.title: Data From a Recent Survey of Political Trends
subfiles.from: Public Opinion and Sociological Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: The report presents results of an October 1949 national survey of cabinet and party support.
subfiles.summary: The survey finds substantial support for the Yoshida Cabinet and the Democratic Liberal Party, with the Social Democrats second in stated voting preference. Tables compare support across parties and occupations and track shifts since January. A note cautions that respondents may conceal Communist sympathies.

subfiles.title: Filipino Attitude Toward Post-war Japan: transmittal of Neri address
subfiles.from: Evett D. Hester, chargé d’affaires ad interim, Manila
subfiles.about: Hester forwards Neri’s address and explains Philippine conditions for supporting Japan’s international return.
subfiles.summary: Hester emphasizes Philippine reparations claims and opposition to renewed Japanese dominance in Asia. He summarizes Neri’s conditions for Japan’s readmission to international society and the wider aims of Philippine foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Secretary Neri’s radio talk on Philippine foreign policy
subfiles.about: Neri sets out Philippine foreign policy objectives amid major international developments.
subfiles.summary: Neri lists the republic’s objectives, including friendly relations, support for the United Nations and self-determination, special ties with the United States, and claims against Japan. He reviews diplomatic and consular expansion, Philippine participation in international bodies, and support for Indonesia and other territories seeking independence. The address continues beyond page 396.
